newsitem.title: FRANCE: Rich nations debate global warming at energy talks.
newsitem.headline: Rich nations debate global warming at energy talks.

text.p: Energy ministers from the world's main industrial powers gathered in Paris on Thursday to debate a global deal to cut pollution blamed for warming the earth's atmosphere.

No new decisions were expected from talks officially set for Friday, but the 24-nation International Energy Agency planned to repeat earlier warnings there would be no easy answers as rich and developing nations strive to hammer out an agreement for signing in Japan later this year, officials said.

The IEA, grouping some of the world's largest oil consumers and originally set up in 1974 to counter OPEC price rises, will also warn that the world should not run down spare oil supplies simply because prices are relatively stable.
"We would like to warn people not to become complacent about oil supply because markets will become increasingly dependent on oil from the Middle East," an IEA spokesman said.

The IEA's Paris secretariat, part of the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), told its biggest member the United States this month it was concerned the government was cutting its own oil stocks just when its huge imports are rising.
The role of governments in energy, often a sticking point among IEA nations, will be debated over an informal dinner in Paris on Thursday.
The IEA believes a scramble to switch away from oil when the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries was at its peak during a 1970s price shock has just about run its course.
But it worries many countries are cutting research spending at a time when demand for urban transport is growing fast.
It also sees investment in cleaner fuels as a vital way of helping countries meet commitments to counter global warming that is produced by belching heat-trapping gases into the atmosphere.
Most IEA members will fail to meet targets set by a 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro that committed developed nations to reducing their emissions of carbon dioxide to 1990 levels by the year 2000.
The targets were not legally binding but negotiations are under way for compulsory goals stretching beyond 2000 to be agreed at high-level talks in Kyoto, Japan, in December.
The IEA is expected to throw its weight behind efforts to commit countries to binding emission standards, but without straying into sensitive negotiations between its own members.

"It is not a decision-making forum, but we want to make sure people who make decisions in Kyoto have a realistic assessment of the importance of energy as a major part of the climate change problem and therefore part of the solution," the IEA spokesman said.
A March declaration likely to be reaffirmed by the ministers contrasts the circumstances of members, seen by some diplomats as a way of keeping prickly climate politics out of the IEA.
The European Union has offered to cut emissions to 15 percent of 1990 levels by 2010, while Washington has not yet given a timetable and coal-rich Australia opposes forced cuts.
The IEA talks are the first since Hungary last year became the first former Communist country to say it would join the organisation.

Non-member China will also unusually be present with a state planning minister, Ye Qing, invited for informal lunch talks on Friday. The IEA expects China's oil imports to soar over the next 15 years. The country is also the world's largest coal producer and widely seen as a major market for energy services.
